note: Source 1 returned thirty rows of modifiers on 'dubstep artists' and no proper name. Source 2 is the one genuinely useful non-Wikipedia source in this pass: 'big apple' at 8,100 and 'south london' at 3,200 came back as entities the topic talks about, which is Big Apple Records in Croydon arriving from a keyword tool rather than from a history book, alongside 'sound system', 'reggae music', 'half time' and 'bbc radio'. Source 3's People Also Ask rows were 'Who is the biggest dubstep artist?', 'Who are the top 10 dubstep artists?', 'What the heck is dubstep?' and 'Who are the OGs of dubstep?' — that last question is the guide's whole thesis and nobody is answering it well. Source 4 is where this genre diverges hardest from every other one in the set: the top consensus list (themetalverse, 25 most popular dubstep artists) is Kayzo, Wooli, Adventure Club, Knife Party, DNMO, Knock2, GRiZ, Nero, Arcando, Seven Lions, Grabbitz, Flux Pavilion, Getter, Excision, Zeds Dead, NGHTMRE, Subtronics, Warriyo, Dylan Matthew, The Fat Rat, Slushii, Deadmau5, SLANDER, Illenium, Skrillex — twenty-five names and not one founder, not one South Londoner, Skrillex last. Source 5 and source 4 share exactly one name between them. That is the two-genres-in-one-word problem the page already argues, arriving as data. Source 6 ranks Trois-Quarts Taxi System (9 sets), Amaliah (9), Scuba (7), Hodge (7), Spray (7), Martyn (7), James Blake (6), Skream (6), Appleblim (5), Cooly G (5), Plastician (4), Kahn (4). en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward%3E%3E and /wiki/FWD%3E%3E both return 404; the Forward>> material used below is the section inside the dubstep article.

required_records.title: Midnight Request Line
required_records.why: source 5 treats it as the pivot the rest of the decade is measured against — "Building on the success of Skream's grimey anthem 'Midnight Request Line'" — and returns Skream again as "one of the most widely known names on the scene". Also 6 sets in our own catalogue, so Skream is one of only two names returned by both source 5 and source 6

required_records.title: Night
required_records.why: source 5: "Benga and Coki scoring a crossover hit (in a similar manner to Skream's 'Midnight Request Line') with the track 'Night'". The crossover section cannot make its argument without the record the source names as the crossover

required_records.title: Anti War Dub
required_records.why: source 5 calls Mala "one of the pioneers of dubstep music" and credits the pair directly — "Digital Mystikz brought an expanded palette of sounds and influences to the genre, most prominently reggae and dub, as well as orchestral melodies" — and names the DMZ night, DMZ Records and Deep Medi Musik to them. FIGURES.md requires a founder to be audible, not listed; this is the record that does it

required_records.title: Mud
required_records.why: source 5 names Loefah in the founding collective sentence — "the South London collective Digital Mystikz (Mala and Coki), along with labelmates and collaborators Loefah and MC Sgt Pokes" — and again as the founder of Swamp81. The half-step end of the sound has one witness and this is it

required_records.title: Archangel
required_records.why: source 5's Mercury sentence is about the album this track opens — "Burial's late 2007 release Untrue (which was nominated for the 2008 Nationwide Mercury Music Prize)" — and it separately records the self-titled album as The Wire's Best Album of 2006. Untrue is named in the prose; this is the record that plays it

required_records.title: Scary Monsters and Nice Sprites
required_records.why: the only name source 4 and source 5 both return. Source 5: "the harsher electro-house and heavy metal-influenced variant brostep, led by American producers such as Skrillex, boosted dubstep's popularity in the United States", with the EP charting at number three. The page's central argument is that one word covers two musics; this is the second one, and it has to be playable or the argument is one-sided

required_records.title: Concrete Jungle
required_records.why: source 5 calls City Limits Vol. 1 'an influential album' on Deep Medi Musik. The label was named twice on the page and represented by nobody but its founder; this is the album's opening track, from the artist's official channel.

required_records.title: I LOVE: DUBSTEP
required_records.why: source 5 credits Rinse twice in the sentences that matter and the page returned zero hits for the station. A scene is described, so the medium is a set from our own catalogue rather than a record: this Rinse show carries Hatcha and Plastician, both of whom the page had dropped.

known_gaps.title: Trois-Quarts Taxi System; Amaliah; Scuba; Hodge; Spray; Martyn; James Blake; Appleblim; Cooly G
known_gaps.why: catalogue-only, and by FIGURES.md differentiators rather than errors: the names actually playing this music across 62,877 sets, none of which appears on any competing canon list. Cooly G in particular is a Hyperdub artist the histories skip and the catalogue does not. Recorded so the next pass does not re-derive them.

known_gaps.title: Gorgon Sound — Horsepower Productions; Spongebob — Coki; Qawwali — Pinch; Blood On My Hands — Shackleton; Yasuo — Bommer & Crowell; Worlds Apart — Seven Lions
known_gaps.why: not gaps. All six are embedded on the page and none was returned as a record by three sources or by source 5, so they are recorded here to stop a later pass reading their absence from the required list as an error. Shackleton and Coki are both source 5 names carried by records source 5 does not name, which is the writer's judgement and the algorithm does not overrule it.
